cells.tense: You are on the crossing now, and your hand is still on the pen that keeps it level.
cells.act: rest in the balance you already have
cells.ask: Pick an arrangement you keep evening out by hand. Nothing gets touched for an afternoon. Let it run while you sit inside the evenness you built.
cells.core:
You are walking toward something that matters, and the footing under it is level. Weight is shared, no one carries more than they give, and because the load is spread, the crossing does not hang on any single person's stamina. It looks unremarkable when it works: people say the true thing, small gaps get closed, and you aren't the one holding the whole weight up. Nothing goes unfed while you aren't watching.

The catch is that you keep working it. You watch who gave what and close the gaps before anybody feels them. That labor is real, and it is also the last labor needed here. Set an arrangement down for an afternoon and take your hand off it. What you built is solid enough to sit inside. Rest in the balance you already have, rather than guarding it.
cells.sheetLine: The balance is even, and it no longer needs your hands.

cells.tense: You will reach the far edge soon, and you are already bracing for how it will be fair.
cells.act: start building where the false thing fell
cells.ask: Before the next hard talk about who owes what, sketch what you would make once that talk is finished. A line or two on a page. Then set the pen down.
cells.core:
What is owed has become the question you check before every step. Who gave, who gets credit, who will say you took too much — the arithmetic runs ahead of you into country you haven't reached. You can't arrive anywhere while pre-auditing the arrival, and the people beside you feel the scale hanging over the room before anyone speaks.

What is under it is real: you are at a crossing, and you want the walk clean. But a crossing is crossed, not pre-cleaned. So start building where the false thing fell. A sketch, a line — not a plan, just something that could exist on the far side. It won't settle the fairness question. It gives your walk a direction, so you are moving toward something instead of away from a scale.
cells.sheetLine: Weighing every step is how a crossing stops happening.

cells.tense: You stood at this threshold once, and your weight is still back on the old side.
cells.act: work the pattern through to its logic
cells.ask: Take some place where you give more than you receive, and follow it to its logical end on paper before you change anything. See where it leads.
cells.core:
There is a crossing ahead of you and you are not on it. What carried you this far is behind, the step forward hasn't started, and your weight rests on the old bank. The fairness in your days runs the same way: you give, you smooth, you take the short end, and you have stopped noticing it as anything at all. Offers arrive and pass through.

So don't fix it. Work the pattern through to its logic. A place where you give more than you get — follow it to its end on paper, nothing more. The tracing does its own work: once the shape is visible it stops being invisible, and the first even step has somewhere to start. You are not being asked to give less. You are being asked to look before you move.
cells.sheetLine: You give more than you get, and you've stopped counting it.

cells.tense: You are the one holding this crossing level, and asked, you'd say it just stayed level.
cells.ask: Let an hour pass without evening anything out between people. When the urge comes, notice it, and leave the scale alone for that hour.
cells.core:
There is a crossing in your life and it has stayed level — people treated squarely, nobody left holding more than their share, small repairs made before anyone spotted a crack. You'd call the group good at that, fair without help. But if you think about the last time it wobbled, you remember quietly stepping in. Your hand is on the tiller. You file it under how things happen to go.

Seeing it is the only difference here. Let an hour pass without adjusting anything, and when the urge to even something out arrives, notice it and leave the scale alone. Then let your mind go quiet and either return or don't. Both are fine. The truth stands whether you name it: you have been steering the balance, and it is yours to see.
cells.sheetLine: The evenness you credit to the room is your hand on the tiller.

A reader could reasonably say 'I'm not leaving anything, I'm just tired of the same conversations,' and the Too Much cell's over-fairness and the Too Little cell's one-way giving both still stand as descriptions of the seat, not of a departure. The asks survive being wrong: each is one small act on the person's own adjustment, and if the read is off, the act still teaches them something about where their calibration runs. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you're meant to walk on' — it flatters the reader's map, so it is not in the cells; the crossing is stated as a direction, never as a verdict on anyone.
